presentingComplaint: Sudden onset palpitations and breathlessness for 6 hours, associated with lightheadedness.
history: A 68-year-old woman with known hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with abrupt onset of rapid, irregular palpitations that began 6 hours ago while she was resting. She describes associated mild breathlessness on exertion and one episode of near-syncope while standing up, but no true loss of consciousness. No chest pain. She denies fever, cough, or recent illness. She reports two similar but self-terminating episodes of palpitations over the past 3 months, each lasting under an hour, which she did not seek care for. She has never been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation before. No history of thyroid disease, alcohol excess, or recent stimulant/caffeine binge. She takes amlodipine and metformin; no anticoagulants. No history of stroke or bleeding.
examination: Alert and mildly anxious, in no acute distress. Pulse irregularly irregular at 138/min, weaker in volume with beat-to-beat variation; pulse deficit noted on apical-radial comparison. Blood pressure 108/68 mmHg. JVP not elevated. Precordial exam: irregular rhythm, no murmurs, normal S1/S2 intensity variation consistent with AF. Chest clear to auscultation, no crackles. No peripheral edema. No focal neurological deficit. No goiter or thyroid enlargement.
imaging: 12-lead ECG: absence of P waves, irregularly irregular narrow QRS rhythm at ~140/min consistent with atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, no acute ST-T ischemic changes
Chest X-ray: normal cardiac silhouette, no pulmonary edema
Transthoracic echocardiogram (pending): to assess left atrial size, LV function, and valvular disease
differentialDiagnoses: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Sinus tachycardia secondary to underlying stressor
Acute coronary syndrome with arrhythmic presentation
finalDiagnosis: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (new-onset, hemodynamically stable)
citations: Harrison 22e — Chapter on Atrial Fibrillation and Other Supraventricular Arrhythmias
ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation 2024
contraindications: Avoid AV nodal blocking agents (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) if pre-excitation (WPW) is suspected — assess ECG for delta waves first
Anticoagulation decisions must weigh bleeding risk (e.g., use HAS-BLED) against stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc), especially before cardioversion strategies
Rhythm control with cardioversion contraindicated without adequate anticoagulation or TEE exclusion of atrial thrombus if AF duration >48h or unknown
edgeCases: If patient becomes hemodynamically unstable (hypotension, altered sensorium, ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure), urgent synchronized DC cardioversion is indicated regardless of anticoagulation status

Unknown duration of AF (given prior undiagnosed self-terminating episodes) mandates a rate-control-first strategy with anticoagulation rather than immediate rhythm control, per AHA/ACC/HRS and ESC guidance
CHA2DS2-VASc score in this patient (age ≥65, hypertension, diabetes, female sex) is ≥3, indicating a clear indication for long-term oral anticoagulation regardless of rhythm control strategy
expectedMaiK: New-onset AF with RVR in a hemodynamically stable patient — prioritize rate control, calculate CHA2DS2-VASc for anticoagulation decision, and evaluate for reversible precipitants (thyroid, electrolytes, ischemia) before considering rhythm control given uncertain AF duration.
